Title: Patient Contrastive Learning: a Performant, Expressive, and Practical Approach to ECG Modeling.
Abstract: Supervised machine learning applications in health care are often limited due to a scarcity of labeled training data. To mitigate this effect small sample size, we introduce pre-training approach, Patient Contrastive Learning Representations (PCLR), which creates latent representations ECGs from large number unlabeled examples. The resulting expressive, performant, and practical across wide spectrum clinical tasks. We develop PCLR using system with over 3.2 million 12-lead ECGs, demonstrate substantial improvements multiple new tasks when there fewer than 5,000 labels.

Title: Screening for cardiac contractile dysfunction using an artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiogram
Abstract: Asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction (ALVD) is present in 3-6% of the general population, is associated with reduced quality of life and longevity, and is treatable when found1-4. An inexpensive, noninvasive screening tool for ALVD in the doctor's office is not available. We tested the hypothesis that application of artificial intelligence (AI) to the electrocardiogram (ECG), a routine method of measuring the heart's electrical activity, could identify ALVD. Using paired 12-lead ECG and echocardiogram data, including the left ventricular ejection fraction (a measure of contractile function), from 44,959 patients at the Mayo Clinic, we trained a convolutional neural network to identify patients with ventricular dysfunction, defined as ejection fraction ≤35%, using the ECG data alone. When tested on an independent set of 52,870 patients, the network model yielded values for the area under the curve, sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy of 0.93, 86.3%, 85.7%, and 85.7%, respectively. In patients without ventricular dysfunction, those with a positive AI screen were at 4 times the risk (hazard ratio, 4.1; 95% confidence interval, 3.3 to 5.0) of developing future ventricular dysfunction compared with those with a negative screen. Application of AI to the ECG-a ubiquitous, low-cost test-permits the ECG to serve as a powerful screening tool in asymptomatic individuals to identify ALVD.

gold.abstract: Electrocardiograms (ECGs) are an established technique to screen for abnormal cardiac signals. Recent work has established that it is possible to detect arrhythmia directly from the ECG signal using deep learning algorithms. While a few prior approaches with contrastive learning have been successful, the best way to define a positive sample remains an open question. In this project, we investigate several ways to define positive samples, and assess which approach yields the best performance in a downstream task of classifying arrhythmia. We explore spatiotemporal invariances, generic augmentations, demographic similarities, cardiac rhythms, and wave attributes of ECG as potential ways to match positive samples. We then evaluate each strategy with downstream task performance, and find that learned representations invariant to patient identity are powerful in arrhythmia detection. We made our code available in: https://github.com/mandiehyewon/goodviews_ecg.git

These are your colleagues' latest proposals:

--- Researcher B ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- PCLR: a contrastive pre-training method that learns ECG representations from >3.2 million unlabeled 12-lead ECGs and improves clinical tasks when fewer than 5,000 labels are available.
- Mayo AI-ECG: a supervised CNN trained on paired ECG-echocardiogram data detects asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction (ALVD; EF ≤35%) with AUC 0.93, sensitivity 86.3%, specificity 85.7%, and identifies patients without baseline dysfunction at 4.1 times higher risk of future dysfunction.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
PCLR supplies transferable ECG representations that reduce dependence on scarce labeled echocardiograms. The ALVD task supplies a clinically meaningful, validated outcome. Fine-tuning PCLR on a small labeled ECG-echo subset operatively connects self-supervised representation learning to low-label detection of contractile dysfunction and future ALVD risk.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Use PCLR pre-trained on large unlabeled 12-lead ECGs. From the Mayo-labeled ECG-echo cohort underlying the ALVD paper, create a low-label training subset of ≤5,000 ECGs. Fine-tune PCLR to predict EF ≤35% and compare against a de novo CNN and the published 0.93 AUC. Metrics: AUC, sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, calibration. Secondary endpoint: among patients with baseline EF >35%, compare risk of future EF ≤35% for positive versus negative PCLR screens using hazard ratios. Validate on an independent held-out set. Missing cross-paper knowledge: exact overlap between PCLR pre-training data and the Mayo echo cohort; whether PCLR representations encode subtle contractile dysfunction before supervised fine-tuning; external-site generalizability.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
This project tests whether contrastive ECG pre-training improves screening for asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction when labeled echocardiogram data are scarce. PCLR will be fine-tuned on ≤5,000 paired ECG-echo records to detect EF ≤35%, with comparison against de novo CNN training and published performance. We also evaluate whether PCLR-based positive screens predict future ventricular dysfunction. The contribution is a sample-efficient, clinically validated ECG screen combining unlabeled representation learning with contractile dysfunction detection, moving beyond either paper alone.

FINAL IDEA: Fine-tuning PCLR’s contrastive ECG representations on a small labeled ECG-echo subset provides a sample-efficient screening tool for asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction and future contractile decline.

--- Researcher C ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper-b (PCLR): Contrastive self-supervised pre-training on >3.2 million unlabeled 12-lead ECGs creates general ECG representations; downstream tasks improve with fewer than 5,000 labels.
- Paper-c (Mayo AI-ECG): Supervised CNN on paired ECG-echocardiogram data from 44,959 patients detects EF≤35% from ECG alone (AUC 0.93; sensitivity 86.3%; specificity 85.7%); positive screen in normal-EF patients confers hazard ratio 4.1 for future ventricular dysfunction.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Use PCLR’s unsupervised ECG representations as the backbone for the ALVD screening task, then fine-tune with a small number of echocardiogram labels. Operationally, contrastive pre-training from unlabeled ECGs supplies a cardiac-electrical feature space; supervised echo labels align that space to contractile function. This should reduce required paired ECG-echo labels and allow probing of whether latent electrical remodeling precedes overt EF decline.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Reimplement PCLR on available unlabeled 12-lead ECGs. Using Mayo paired ECG-echo data, create label-scarce training subsets (100, 250, 500, 1,000, 5,000 patients) labeled EF≤35% vs >35%. Compare PCLR-fine-tuned models against a supervised CNN trained from scratch on the same subsets. Validate on an independent set with AUC, sensitivity/specificity at a fixed specificity threshold, and calibration. Longitudinal validation: among baseline EF>35% patients, compare incident EF≤35% hazard for positive vs negative PCLR screen. Missing cross-paper knowledge: no access to PCLR code/weights, pretraining corpus overlap with Mayo data, or paired echo labels beyond paper-c.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We propose combining contrastive self-supervised ECG pre-training with AI-ECG detection of low ejection fraction. The hypothesis is that PCLR representations require substantially fewer echo-labeled ECGs to match Mayo’s supervised CNN and that PCLR-positive normal-EF patients show elevated risk of future contractile dysfunction.

FINAL IDEA: Contrastive self-supervised ECG representations reduce label requirements for AI-ECG detection of low ejection fraction and enable early risk stratification for future contractile dysfunction.
